questions.question: What is the purpose of web scraping?
options: To create new websites from scratch
To automatically extract specific data from websites
To design the visual layout of web pages
To execute JavaScript code in a browser
questions.explanation: Web scraping is the automated process of extracting specific data from websites, like product prices, news headlines, or contact information, without manual copying and pasting.

questions.question: In HTML, what is the difference between a tag and an attribute?
options: Tags define elements (like `<a>`); attributes provide extra information about the element (like `href`)
Tags are always visible; attributes are hidden
Attributes define elements; tags provide extra information
There is no difference; they are the same thing
questions.explanation: Tags (like `<a>`, `<div>`, `<h1>`) define the elements themselves. Attributes (like `href`, `class`, `id`) are added to tags to provide additional information or functionality.

questions.question: Why are `class` and `id` attributes important for web scraping?
options: They make the website load faster
They act like 'GPS coordinates' to help locate specific elements on a page
They are required for all HTML tags to work
They automatically download the content
questions.explanation: Classes and IDs are unique identifiers that help you pinpoint exact elements in a page. While many elements might share the same tag name (like 50 `<div>` tags), a specific `id` is usually unique, making it much easier to target the exact data you want.

questions.question: What is the purpose of setting a 'User-Agent' header in a web scraping request?
options: To encrypt the data being sent
To make the script identify itself as a regular web browser
To automatically parse the HTML response
To increase the download speed
questions.explanation: The User-Agent header tells the server what kind of client is making the request. By setting it to mimic a standard browser (like Chrome or Firefox), you can avoid being blocked by websites that try to prevent automated scripts.

questions.question: What is the difference between `response.text` and `response.content` in the requests library?
options: `.text` returns a string; `.content` returns bytes
`.text` returns bytes; `.content` returns a string
They are identical and can be used interchangeably
`.text` is for HTML; `.content` is for CSS
questions.explanation: `.text` returns the response content as a string (used for HTML and text). `.content` returns the content as raw bytes (used for downloading binary files like images, PDFs, etc.).

questions.question: What does `response.raise_for_status()` do?
options: It prints the status code to the console
It automatically raises an exception if the request returned an error status (4xx or 5xx)
It raises the request priority in the network queue
It converts the response to JSON format
questions.explanation: `raise_for_status()` is a convenient method that checks if the request was successful. If the status code indicates an error (like 404 or 500), it automatically raises an exception, preventing your code from trying to process a failed response.

questions.question: What is the purpose of BeautifulSoup in web scraping?
options: To download HTML files from the internet
To convert raw HTML strings into a searchable Python object
To render JavaScript on web pages
To automatically fill out web forms
questions.explanation: BeautifulSoup takes the messy HTML string obtained from requests and builds a structured Python object that mimics the DOM tree, making it easy to navigate and search for specific elements.

questions.question: What is the difference between `soup.find('div')` and `soup.find_all('div')`?
options: `find()` returns the first matching element; `find_all()` returns a list of all matching elements
`find()` works with tags; `find_all()` works with attributes
They are identical and can be used interchangeably
`find()` returns a string; `find_all()` returns a BeautifulSoup object
questions.explanation: `find()` returns the first matching element (a single Tag object). `find_all()` returns a list of all matching Tag objects, which you typically loop through to access each element.

questions.question: Why does BeautifulSoup use `class_` (with an underscore) instead of `class` when searching by CSS class?
options: It's a typo in the library
`class` is a reserved keyword in Python, so it cannot be used as a parameter name
The underscore makes the search faster
It only works with classes that have underscores in their names
questions.explanation: In Python, `class` is a reserved keyword used to define classes. BeautifulSoup uses `class_` (with an underscore) to avoid conflicting with this keyword when you want to search by CSS class.

questions.question: What would be the correct way to access the `href` attribute from a BeautifulSoup Tag object `link`?
options: `link.get_attribute('href')`
`link['href']`
`link.href`
`link.attr('href')`
questions.explanation: BeautifulSoup Tag objects behave like dictionaries. You can access attributes using square brackets: `tag['attribute_name']`.

questions.question: Why is searching by `id` often more reliable than searching by tag name?
options: `id` attributes are always visible in the HTML
`id` is designed to be unique to a single element on a page
`id` is faster to search programmatically
`id` works with all HTML tags
questions.explanation: An `id` attribute is meant to be unique within a webpage. While a page might have 50 `<div>` tags, it should only have one element with a specific `id`, making it perfect for pinpointing exactly one piece of data.

questions.question: Why does BeautifulSoup use `class_` (with an underscore) instead of `class` when searching by CSS class?
options: It's a typo that became standard
`class` is a reserved keyword in Python, so it can't be used as a parameter name
The underscore makes the search case-insensitive
It only works with classes that have underscores in their names
questions.explanation: In Python, `class` is a reserved keyword used to define classes. BeautifulSoup uses `class_` (with an underscore) to avoid conflicting with this keyword when you want to search by CSS class.

questions.question: What is the benefit of chaining `find()` calls (e.g., finding a container first, then searching within it)?
options: It makes the code run faster
It narrows the search scope, preventing matches from outside the relevant section
It automatically converts results to strings
It's the only way to find elements by class
questions.explanation: Chaining allows you to first locate a specific container element (like a product listing div), and then search only within that container. This prevents your scraper from accidentally picking up similar elements from other parts of the page (like navigation menus or footers).

questions.question: What would be the most precise way to find all anchor tags (`<a>`) that have the class `'nav-link'`?
options: `soup.find_all('a', class='nav-link')`
`soup.find_all('a', class_='nav-link')`
`soup.find_all(class_='nav-link')`
`soup.find_all('a').find_all(class_='nav-link')`
questions.explanation: The most precise method is to specify both the tag name and the class: `soup.find_all('a', class_='nav-link')`. This ensures you only get anchor tags with that specific class, ignoring any other elements that might use the same class name.
